questions.stem: Which is a typical challenge of the start-up stage of the business life cycle?
options: defending market share against many new imitators
deciding whether to sell a business whose sales are declining
coordinating offices in several overseas countries
managing cash flow while sales are still building
questions.explanation: In start-up, costs are high and sales are still building, so cash flow is a key challenge, along with building a customer base and setting up systems. Defending share and decline belong to later stages.

questions.stem: In a franchise agreement, the franchisor is:
options: the person who buys the right to operate one outlet under the brand's name and system
the government agency that approves every new franchise outlet
the bank that lends money to buy the franchise outlet
the business that owns the brand and system and sells the right to use them
questions.explanation: The franchisor owns the brand, products and operating system and licenses them to franchisees. The franchisee buys the right to run an outlet using that system.

questions.stem: Which is a usual responsibility of the franchisee?
options: developing new products for every outlet in the franchise network
setting the royalties and fees that all the other franchisees in the network must pay
running the outlet day to day and following the franchisor's operating standards
designing the national advertising campaigns for the whole brand
questions.explanation: Franchisees operate their own outlet within the franchisor's rules on products, presentation and service. The franchisor usually handles brand-wide marketing, product development and the fee structure.

questions.stem: Which costs does a franchisee typically pay?
options: a share of the franchisor's company tax and its directors' salaries
nothing at all, because the franchisor pays every cost in return for the brand's growth
an initial franchise fee, ongoing royalties and a contribution to a marketing fund
only a single payment at the start, with no further fees ever charged
questions.explanation: Franchisees usually pay an upfront fee for the right to the brand, ongoing royalties, often a percentage of sales, and a levy for national marketing, as well as fit-out and running costs.

questions.stem: Under the Franchising Code of Conduct, why must a franchisor give a prospective franchisee a disclosure document before the agreement is signed?
options: so the franchisee is legally prevented from seeking any outside advice
so the franchise is automatically registered as a public company
so the franchisee can make an informed decision about the costs, risks and obligations
so the franchisor can avoid any legal responsibility for the statements it has made to buyers
questions.explanation: The Code, a mandatory industry code under the Competition and Consumer Act 2010, requires disclosure so franchisees understand fees, the franchisor's history and their obligations. Franchisees are encouraged to get legal and financial advice.

questions.stem: Using the business criteria, which comparison of joining a fast-food franchise with opening an independent café is most valid?
options: the two pathways carry the same risk because both are new businesses
the franchise offers a proven system and brand, but fees and rules limit profit and independence
the franchise is always more efficient, because franchisees never pay any ongoing fees or royalties
the independent café is always more competitive because it has a known brand
questions.explanation: A franchise reduces risk through a tested system, training and brand recognition, but royalties reduce profit and the franchisee has less freedom. An independent café has full control but must build its brand from nothing.

questions.stem: Using the Australian Bureau of Statistics' employee-based definition, a small business employs:
options: fewer than 5 people
fewer than 20 people
fewer than 200 people
fewer than 100 people
questions.explanation: The ABS classifies businesses with fewer than 20 employees as small, 20 to 199 as medium and 200 or more as large. Fewer than 5 is often described as a micro business within the small category.

questions.stem: Under Queensland's Work Health and Safety Act 2011, a person conducting a business or undertaking must:
options: leave all safety decisions to the workers themselves
provide safety training only to workers who request it
ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health and safety of workers
guarantee that no worker is ever injured at work in any circumstances at all
questions.explanation: The Act places the primary duty on the person conducting the business or undertaking to ensure health and safety so far as is reasonably practicable, which includes safe systems, training and supervision. It cannot require a guarantee that no one is ever hurt.

questions.stem: A new Queensland business is about to hire its first employees. Which insurance must it generally hold?
options: car insurance for every employee's private vehicle
workers' compensation insurance with WorkCover Queensland
public liability insurance with the Australian Taxation Office
income protection insurance for the owner only
questions.explanation: Queensland employers generally must hold a workers' compensation policy with WorkCover Queensland to cover workers injured at work. Public liability insurance is advisable but is not provided by the ATO.

questions.stem: A new food manufacturer follows the food safety standards set for its industry and an industry code of practice. What is the main purpose of standards and codes of practice?
options: they replace the need for the business to comply with any legislation at all
they apply only to public companies listed on the stock exchange
they are marketing slogans that do not affect operations
they set out practical ways to meet legal requirements and expected quality
questions.explanation: Standards and codes of practice give detailed, practical guidance on meeting safety, quality and legal obligations. Following them helps show compliance; they do not replace the law.

questions.stem: Which correctly matches the POLC responsibilities of a manager?
options: producing, ordering, listing and checking
planning, organising, leading and controlling
pricing, operating, lending and contracting
promoting, outsourcing, licensing and costing
questions.explanation: POLC stands for planning (setting objectives and strategies), organising (arranging resources), leading (motivating and directing people) and controlling (monitoring and correcting performance).

questions.stem: The owner of a new Cairns dive shop compares actual weekly sales with the budget and takes action when sales fall short. Which POLC responsibility is this?
options: organising
leading
controlling
planning
questions.explanation: Controlling involves measuring performance against plans and taking corrective action. Setting the budget in the first place was planning.

questions.stem: Before opening, the owner of a new bakery decides who will bake, who will serve customers and when each person will work. Which POLC responsibility is this?
options: planning
organising
controlling
leading
questions.explanation: Organising means arranging people, tasks and resources so plans can be carried out. Controlling happens later, when performance is checked.

questions.stem: A start-up manager motivates her small team through regular encouragement and by clearly communicating the business's goals. Which POLC responsibility is this?
options: organising
controlling
planning
leading
questions.explanation: Leading involves influencing, motivating and communicating with staff. Organising is about arranging resources and roles.

questions.stem: Which correctly lists the stages of the employment cycle?
options: planning, organising, leading and controlling
seed, start-up, growth and maturity
recruitment, promotion, retirement and rehiring
acquisition, development, maintenance and separation
questions.explanation: The employment cycle covers acquiring staff, developing them through training, maintaining them through pay, conditions and relations, and separation when they leave. POLC and the life cycle are other models.

questions.stem: A new business sends its staff on a customer service course. Which stage of the employment cycle is this?
options: maintenance
development
acquisition
separation
questions.explanation: Training builds employees' skills, which is the development stage. Acquisition is recruiting and selecting, and separation is when employees leave.

questions.stem: A business offers competitive pay, flexible hours and recognition awards to keep good staff. Which stage of the employment cycle is this?
options: development
acquisition
separation
maintenance
questions.explanation: Maintenance involves the pay, benefits, conditions and relationships that keep employees satisfied and retained. Development focuses on building skills.

questions.stem: A new Ipswich business needs two skilled technicians quickly. Option A: a recruitment agency (fast, wide reach, high fee). Option B: its own social media post (cheap, but uncertain reach). Using business criteria, which recommendation is most justified?
options: Option A, as filling the roles quickly with qualified staff outweighs the extra cost
Option B, as the cheapest option is always the most effective one for a start-up business
Option A, as agencies guarantee that every candidate will stay for many years
Option B, as social media posts always reach more qualified people than agencies
questions.explanation: When roles are urgent and skilled, effectiveness in finding suitable staff quickly can justify the agency's fee. Cheapness alone does not make a strategy effective, and no method guarantees retention.

questions.stem: How do human resources objectives help a start-up achieve its business goals?
options: having the right number of skilled, motivated staff lets the business deliver its products and service
they ensure that the business never needs to pay any wages or superannuation in its first year of trading
they replace the need for financial and marketing objectives
they are only relevant once a business reaches the maturity stage
questions.explanation: Objectives such as hiring skilled staff and keeping turnover low support goals like customer satisfaction and growth. HR objectives work alongside financial and marketing objectives from the start.

questions.stem: Which is an example of short-term finance for a start-up business?
options: a 10-year loan used to buy production machinery
a bank overdraft used to cover gaps in cash flow
a 25-year mortgage used to buy business premises
an investor buying a 30% share of the business
questions.explanation: Short-term finance is repaid within a year and suits working capital needs, such as an overdraft or trade credit. Mortgages and long-term loans suit non-current assets, and an investor's share is equity.

questions.stem: Why should a start-up use long-term finance, rather than an overdraft, to buy equipment it will use for ten years?
options: long-term finance never charges interest, unlike an overdraft
an overdraft cannot legally be used by any small business
long-term finance does not need to be repaid at all if the business later fails or closes
repayments are spread over the period the equipment earns income, protecting cash flow
questions.explanation: Matching the finance to the life of the asset spreads repayments over the years the asset generates revenue, avoiding a cash flow squeeze. Long-term loans still charge interest and must be repaid.

questions.stem: What is the main role of budgeting in the strategic planning of a start-up business?
options: to record the business's actual transactions in the journals after they have already taken place
to guarantee that the business will make a profit in its first year
to set the prices charged by the business's competitors
to estimate start-up costs, revenue and cash flow so the owner can plan and control finances
questions.explanation: Budgets forecast income and spending, showing how much finance is needed and providing targets against which actual results are compared. Recording actual transactions is bookkeeping.

questions.stem: Liquidity, as a financial objective, refers to a business's ability to:
options: pay its short-term debts as they fall due
pay all of its debts, including long-term debts, over time
earn a profit from its sales and assets
increase its size and sales over time
questions.explanation: Liquidity is about short-term cash availability. Paying all debts over the long term is solvency, earning profit is profitability, and getting bigger is growth.

questions.stem: A start-up aims to reduce the cost of producing each unit by cutting wasted materials. Which financial objective is this?
options: efficiency
solvency
liquidity
growth
questions.explanation: Efficiency is about using resources well to keep costs per unit low. Solvency and liquidity are about paying debts, and growth is about increasing size.

questions.stem: A start-up has borrowed heavily and its total liabilities now exceed its total assets. Which financial objective is most at risk?
options: profitability
solvency
efficiency
growth
questions.explanation: Solvency is the ability to meet all debts in the long term; liabilities above assets means the business could not pay everything it owes. It may still be profitable or efficient in the short run.

questions.stem: How can joining a professional association help a start-up business?
options: it gives access to industry information, training, advice and contacts
it guarantees the business a share of the association's members' customers
it removes the business's legal obligations under employment law
it provides free finance that never needs to be repaid
questions.explanation: Professional and industry associations are strategic networks offering updates on regulation, training, events and connections with peers. They do not guarantee customers or replace legal obligations.

questions.stem: Compared with PEST, the STEEPLE analytical tool adds which factors?
options: economic, political and sociocultural
effectiveness, location and equity
environmental, legal and ethical
efficiency, leadership and employees
questions.explanation: STEEPLE covers sociocultural, technological, economic, environmental, political, legal and ethical factors. Economic, political and sociocultural factors are already part of PEST.

questions.stem: In a STEEPLE analysis for a new Gold Coast clothing label, growing public concern about workers' conditions in overseas factories belongs under:
options: technological
economic
political
ethical
questions.explanation: Questions of fairness and doing the right thing by workers are ethical factors. If a new law required supply chain reporting, that change would be legal.

questions.stem: A STEEPLE analysis for a planned Brisbane laundromat shows rising electricity prices, stricter water-use regulations and more people living in apartments without laundries. What is the most valid conclusion?
options: the business should not open, because two of the three factors are negative
the trends have no implication, because a laundromat is not affected by its environment
only the apartment trend matters, since rising costs and new regulations can be ignored by small businesses
demand looks strong, but energy- and water-efficient machines will be needed to control costs and comply
questions.explanation: Interpreting the factors together shows a sociocultural trend favouring demand, alongside economic and legal pressures the business can address through efficient equipment. Small businesses must also comply with regulations.

questions.stem: The break-even point is the level of sales at which:
options: variable costs equal fixed costs
the selling price equals the variable cost per unit
total revenue equals total costs, so there is neither profit nor loss
the business makes the highest possible profit for the year
questions.explanation: At break-even, revenue exactly covers fixed and variable costs. Above it the business makes a profit, and below it a loss.

questions.stem: A candle maker sells candles for $30 each. Variable costs are $12 per candle and fixed costs are $54,000 a year. Using break-even units = fixed costs ÷ (price − variable cost), how many candles must it sell to break even?
questions.explanation: Contribution per candle = 30 − 12 = $18, and 54,000 ÷ 18 = 3,000 candles. Dividing by the price alone gives 1,800, and dividing by the variable cost gives 4,500.

questions.stem: The candle maker wants a profit of $18,000. How many candles must it sell?
questions.explanation: Units = (fixed costs + target profit) ÷ contribution = (54,000 + 18,000) ÷ 18 = 4,000 candles. Adding the profit but dividing by the $30 price gives a much smaller figure.

questions.stem: If the candle maker raises its price to $36 while costs stay the same, what happens to the break-even point, and what is the main risk?
options: it falls to 1,500 candles, and there is no risk because profit must rise
it falls to 2,250 candles, but the higher price may reduce the number sold
it rises to 4,000 candles, because higher selling prices always increase costs
it stays at 3,000 candles, because fixed costs have not changed
questions.explanation: Contribution rises to 36 − 12 = $24, so break-even = 54,000 ÷ 24 = 2,250 candles. Fewer sales are needed to cover costs, but customers may buy fewer at the higher price, so actual profit depends on demand.
